passage:
Monday, first week of winter term: the new boy, Tushar, walked in on crutches. At break the class played kho-kho, and he sat alone on the steps. Chandrika saw him but ran to her team.
Wednesday: it was cold and foggy, and kho-kho moved indoors. Chandrika noticed Tushar watching every move. She sat beside him. "You know the rules better than us." He shrugged. "I watch a lot."
The next Monday, Chandrika asked Ma'am if Tushar could be the referee and chaser-caller. He blew the whistle and shouted calls sharper than anyone. At the end, two boys argued about a tag, and they both turned to him. "Tushar, was it out?"
He grinned. "Out." Chandrika laughed. Nobody argued.

qa.q: What game did the class play at break?
qa.a: The class played kho-kho.

qa.q: What was Tushar likely feeling sitting alone on the steps?
qa.a: Tushar was likely lonely and left out, watching a game he knew well but wasn't part of.

qa.q: What small step made the biggest difference for Tushar?
qa.a: Chandrika sitting with him, noticing what he was good at, and asking the teacher for a role that fit him.

qa.q: How do the other boys come to see Tushar?
qa.a: They come to trust his judgement, turning to him to settle an argument, so he becomes part of the game.

grounding: Shows a child making room for a new classmate who uses crutches by finding a real role for him.

passage:
During the Baisakhi fair in the village, the school held a kabaddi match. Maria, eleven, lined up with the boys' team.
"Girls can't play kabaddi," Amandeep said, and a few boys snickered. "Go do rangoli."
Maria's jaw tightened. "I can. Ask Coach."
Coach nodded. Maria played two raids and got one point. When she was tagged, she stepped back from the line quickly.
Later Amandeep came over. "You were good. Sorry about the rangoli thing." Then he asked, "Can we shake hands, or is that weird?"
"Handshake's fine," Maria said, holding out her hand. His friend Harjit laughed, and Amandeep laughed too.

qa.q: How many points did Maria get in her raids?
qa.a: She got one point.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling when the boys snickered?
qa.a: Maria felt angry and determined, her jaw tight, ready to prove she belonged in the game.

qa.q: What did Amandeep do well after the match?
qa.a: He apologised for the rangoli comment, praised her play, and asked before shaking hands, which respected her boundaries.

qa.q: How might Harjit see the change in Amandeep?
qa.a: Harjit may be amused and a bit surprised to see his friend go from mocking Maria to apologising and treating her as a teammate.

grounding: Shows children learning courtesy and respect across genders instead of stereotyped roles or mockery.

passage:
The rain was pouring and Irfan's mother had sent him to buy sugar before the Eid guests arrived. The shop was packed, and the shopkeeper, in a hurry, handed Irfan change for a five-hundred note. Irfan had given him a hundred.
Outside, under the awning, Irfan counted it twice. His friend Gurpreet whistled. "Lucky! He'll never know."
Irfan's heart was racing. Nobody had seen. The guests were coming. The rain was getting worse.
He went back in anyway, waited behind four people, and held out the extra notes. "Uncle, you gave me too much."
The shopkeeper stared, then laughed and gave Irfan a toffee. "Your parents raised you well."
Gurpreet shook his head, grinning. "Now I feel bad I said lucky."

qa.q: What note had Irfan given the shopkeeper?
qa.a: He had given him a hundred.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling as he counted the change?
qa.a: He felt nervous and tempted, his heart racing, knowing nobody had seen and he was in a hurry.

qa.q: Why was going back the right choice even though no one saw?
qa.a: Because the money wasn't his, and doing right when no one is watching is what makes a person trustworthy.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet feel after Irfan returns the money?
qa.a: Gurpreet feels a bit ashamed of calling it lucky, but also seems to admire his friend.

grounding: Shows a child being honest about a mistake in his favour even when nobody would find out.

passage:
Deepika, you're upset that the whole class lost games period because one boy broke the window. Let me tell you about the Holi when I was ten.
Our teacher found colour thrown on the notice board. Nobody owned up. So she said all forty of us would clean the school for a week. I was furious. I hadn't even brought colour!
My friend Kamla said, "It's fair. Everyone should share."
I said, "Fair means the punishment fits the person who did it."
We argued all the way home. Then we went together to the teacher and asked if the ones who didn't do it could help find a better way. She listened. The boy who did it came forward the next day.
So, beta, what do you think would be fair this time?

qa.q: How many students were told to clean the school for a week?
qa.a: All forty of them.

qa.q: What was the young storyteller feeling when the whole class was punished?
qa.a: The storyteller felt angry and wronged, because they hadn't even brought colour.

qa.q: What choice in the story changed the outcome?
qa.a: Going together to the teacher to ask for a fairer way, instead of just complaining, led her to listen and the real culprit to come forward.

qa.q: How did Kamla see the class punishment differently?
qa.a: Kamla thought it was fair for everyone to share the consequence, so she saw fairness as equal treatment rather than fitting the person.

grounding: Shows an elder helping a child think about whether a group punishment is proportionate and fair.

passage:
I'm Kishore, Arnab's cousin, and I'm sixteen. At the Durga Puja recitation this year, Arnab, twelve, stood up to read, and his voice cracked in the middle of a line, high then low. Some younger kids giggled. Arnab went red and sat down fast.
After, I found him behind the pandal. He muttered, "Something's wrong with my voice. And I smell weird after football."
I told him mine did the same at his age and that it's just the body growing up. His father came over, heard us, and said gently, "Nothing is wrong. Voices change, sweat changes. A daily bath, clean clothes and a deodorant help. Ask me anything, anytime."
I don't know what Arnab was thinking, but the next evening he read again. His voice cracked once. He kept going.

qa.q: What happened to Arnab's voice during the recitation?
qa.a: His voice cracked in the middle of a line, high then low.

qa.q: What was Arnab probably feeling when he sat down fast?
qa.a: He was probably embarrassed and worried, thinking something was wrong with his body.

qa.q: How did Arnab's father help without making him feel ashamed?
qa.a: He said calmly that the changes were normal, gave simple hygiene tips, and invited Arnab to ask him anything, anytime.

qa.q: How does Kishore's own experience shape the way he helps?
qa.a: Because Kishore went through the same changes, he can reassure his cousin that it's normal and make him feel less alone.

grounding: Shows a child learning about puberty changes and hygiene calmly, without shame or myths.

passage:
Last summer holidays, I practised badminton every morning at six before it got hot. I'm Arohi, and I was twelve. Coach made me do the same backhand drill fifty times a day. It was so boring I cried once.
By the colony tournament in June, my backhand actually worked. I reached the final against Vandana, who is two years older. I lost, 21–17, 21–15.
I wanted to throw my racquet. Instead, I walked to the net and shook Vandana's hand. "Your drop shots are amazing," I said. She smiled. "Your backhand was annoying. In a good way."
Back home I sulked for an hour. Then I asked Coach if I could learn drop shots next.

qa.q: How many times a day did Coach make Arohi do the backhand drill?
qa.a: Coach made Arohi do the same backhand drill fifty times a day.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling after losing the final?
qa.a: Arohi felt frustrated and disappointed, wanting to throw the racquet, and sulked for an hour at home.

qa.q: Which choice showed good sportsmanship, and why?
qa.a: Walking to the net, shaking hands and praising Vandana's drop shots, because it respected the winner even while Arohi felt upset.

qa.q: How might Vandana see Arohi after the match?
qa.a: Vandana probably respects Arohi, both for her improved backhand and for being gracious after losing.

grounding: Shows a child building skill through repeated practice and losing a final gracefully.

passage:
It was exam week in the December cold, and Tenzin had only forty rupees left for the canteen after buying a pen. The chips and a cola cost exactly that. Dal-rice with a boiled egg cost thirty-five.
His friend Leela was already eating chips. "Treat yourself. Exams are stressful."
Tenzin remembered last week: chips at lunch, and by the maths paper at two he was yawning and couldn't think. Amala had said, "Food is fuel, Tenzin. Some fuel burns out fast."
He bought the dal-rice. It wasn't exciting. But at two o'clock, in the chemistry paper, his head felt clear.
Leela, beside him in the hall, was rubbing her eyes. After, she said, "Maybe dal-rice tomorrow."

qa.q: How much did the dal-rice with a boiled egg cost?
qa.a: Dal-rice with a boiled egg cost thirty-five.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin choose dal-rice even though chips were tempting?
qa.a: He was worried about feeling tired and foggy again in his exam, as he had last week after eating chips.

qa.q: What small step could Tenzin keep doing during exams?
qa.a: He could keep choosing filling meals like dal-rice on exam days and save treats for after, noticing how each choice affects his energy.

qa.q: What might Leela realise after the chemistry paper?
qa.a: Leela might realise her tiredness was linked to the chips, which is why she decides to try dal-rice tomorrow.

grounding: Shows a child connecting food choices to energy during exams, despite a tight budget.

passage:
Ayesha, you asked me what to do if someone gets hurt. Let me tell you about the Diwali when your uncle burned his hand. I was twelve, and your Nana was at the shop.
Your uncle grabbed a sparkler by the wrong end and screamed. I froze. Then I remembered what our teacher had drilled into us: stay calm, cool the burn, call for help.
I pulled him to the tap and held his hand under cool running water. I shouted for Mrs Rao next door and asked her to call Nana at the shop. She did. Nana came running and took him to the clinic.
The doctor said we'd done the right first step. I still know that shop number by heart.

qa.q: Whom did the storyteller shout for?
qa.a: The storyteller shouted for Mrs Rao next door.

qa.q: What was the young storyteller feeling when the uncle screamed?
qa.a: The storyteller felt frightened and froze for a second before remembering what the teacher had taught.

qa.q: What choice inside the story made the biggest difference?
qa.a: Staying calm enough to cool the burn under running water and getting a neighbour to call Nana, so an adult took him to the clinic quickly.

qa.q: How might the young uncle have felt when the storyteller acted quickly?
qa.a: He was probably scared and in pain, but relieved and safer because someone knew what to do.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling handling a small burn and knowing whom to call in an emergency as a child.

passage:
The summer I was ten, I went to a craft camp. I'm Aadhya. An older boy who helped the teacher kept trying to make me sit on his lap, and once he touched me where no one is allowed to. He said, "It's our secret."
I remembered what our school counsellor said: private parts are private, secrets that feel bad are not secrets, and keep telling until someone listens.
That evening I told Madhuri Masi. She stopped chopping onions, sat right next to me and listened. She said, "Thank you for telling me. This is not your fault." She called Mumma and the camp director that same night. The director came to our house the next morning, and the boy was removed from the camp.
Masi stayed with me that night. I was scared, but not alone.

qa.q: What did the older boy say about what he did?
qa.a: He said, "It's our secret."

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling after telling Madhuri Masi?
qa.a: Aadhya was still scared but felt safer and not alone, because Masi believed and stayed with her.

qa.q: What did Madhuri Masi do right when Aadhya told her?
qa.a: She stopped what she was doing, listened, said it was not Aadhya's fault, and called Mumma and the camp director the same night.

qa.q: How might the camp director's quick response affect other children at the camp?
qa.a: Removing the boy protects other children too and shows them that adults take such reports seriously.

grounding: Shows a child knowing body boundaries, recognising a bad secret, and telling a trusted adult who acts the same day.

passage:
Yamini, eleven, had been saving her pocket money since the monsoon for a new school bag; the zip on her old one had broken twice. It was nearly Diwali and she had almost enough.
Then, at the Diwali market, with her cousin Abhinav, she saw a glowing slime kit in a stall. Her hand went to her purse.
"Buy it!" said Abhinav. "It's Diwali!"
The crowd pushed, the stall owner said, "Last one!" and Yamini's heart thumped. She thought of the broken zip, the books falling out on the bus.
"Not today," she said, pulling her hand back.
Abhinav rolled his eyes. But two weeks later, when she walked into school with a new bag, he asked, "How did you save for that?"

qa.q: What did Yamini see at the stall?
qa.a: She saw a glowing slime kit.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling when the stall owner said "Last one!"?
qa.a: Yamini felt tempted and pressured, her heart thumping, torn between the fun toy and the bag she needed.

qa.q: How could Yamini handle a moment like this next time?
qa.a: She could remember what she is saving for, as she did with the broken zip, and give herself time before buying rather than deciding in the rush.

qa.q: How does Abhinav's view change by the end?
qa.a: Abhinav first thinks she's being boring, but later is impressed and curious about how she saved for the bag.

grounding: Shows a child choosing a needed item she saved for over a tempting impulse buy during a festival rush.
